context: Writing to house churches in Rome divided between Jewish and Gentile believers, Paul urges each person not to think of himself more highly than he ought but with sober judgment (Rom 12:3), because the church is one body with many members who do not all have the same function (Rom 12:4-5). The gifts (*charismata*) differ according to the grace given, and each is to be exercised wholeheartedly: prophecy in proportion to faith, the giver with generosity, the leader with diligence, the one showing mercy with cheerfulness. The list is weighted toward everyday ministries and leads straight into the call to genuine love (Rom 12:9-21).

The Corinthian church prized spectacular gifts, especially tongues, and ranked believers by them. Paul answers that there are varieties of gifts, services and activities but the same Spirit, Lord and God (1 Cor 12:4-6), and that each manifestation is given for the common good (1 Cor 12:7) and distributed as the Spirit wills (1 Cor 12:11). This list focuses on Spirit-empowered words and works. Whether the more miraculous items continue today is debated: continuationists say they remain until Christ returns (1 Cor 13:8-12), while cessationists argue they authenticated the apostolic era and then ceased.

After the body analogy (1 Cor 12:12-27), Paul lists what God has appointed in the church, ranking the first three ("first apostles, second prophets, third teachers"), perhaps because they ground the church in the word. He then asks a series of questions in Greek that expect the answer "no": not all are apostles, not all speak in tongues. The point is that no single gift, tongues included, is required of everyone, and he immediately turns to "a still more excellent way," love (1 Cor 12:31-13:13). "Helping" and "administrating" (guidance, like steering a ship) appear only here.

Here the gifts are people. Quoting Psalm 68 (Eph 4:8), Paul pictures the ascended Christ distributing gifts to his church. Their purpose is to equip the saints for the work of ministry and build up the body until it reaches unity and maturity (Eph 4:12-16), so ministry belongs to the whole church, not only the leaders. Whether "shepherds and teachers" name one combined role or two overlapping ones is debated, as is whether apostles and prophets continue or were foundational only (Eph 2:20).

Peter writes to scattered and suffering believers in Asia Minor, reminding them that the end of all things is near (1 Pet 4:7). Each has received a gift and should use it to serve others as good stewards of God's varied grace. He groups gifts into two broad kinds: speaking, which should be done as one speaking the very words of God, and serving, which should be done in the strength God supplies, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ. The list is a summary rather than a catalogue.

Isaiah describes a shoot from the stump of Jesse, a coming Davidic ruler on whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest. The Hebrew text names the Spirit and then three pairs: wisdom and understanding, counsel and might, knowledge and the fear of the LORD, adding that he will delight in the fear of the LORD. The Greek Septuagint and Latin Vulgate render the first "fear" as "piety" (godliness), producing a list of seven. On that basis Western church tradition, notably Catholic teaching, speaks of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given to believers, and some link this to the "seven spirits" before God's throne (Rev 1:4). Christians read the passage as fulfilled in Jesus, on whom the Spirit rested (Matt 3:16).
gifts: Piety (in the Greek and Latin tradition)

context: Included for contrast. These are not gifts distributed differently to different believers but the single "fruit" (the noun is singular) that the Spirit grows in every believer. Paul sets it against the "works of the flesh" (Gal 5:19-21) in a letter defending freedom in Christ against those requiring Gentiles to keep the law. Gifts describe what a believer does for others; fruit describes who a believer is becoming. Paul's own warning in 1 Corinthians 13 is that gifts without the fruit of love amount to nothing (1 Cor 13:1-3).
